one_line: Quick anecdotal test of OpenAI's o3-mini and o3-mini-high: the speaker reports correct answers on six reasoning prompts, far faster than o1, plus a Chrome extension built with o3-mini-high.
summary: The host tests OpenAI's o3-mini (standard tier) and o3-mini-high, which OpenAI had just made available in ChatGPT for Plus, Team and Pro users, with free users getting access through a "Reason" option. He cites OpenAI's benchmark claims that o3-mini-high beats o1 on math, PhD-level science and coding, but does not verify them. His own test is six short reasoning prompts (a jug-measuring puzzle, a river crossing, candle blowing order, counting kiwis, word frequency, a probability question), timed by eye and compared against memory of o1's times. He reports correct answers on all of them, with response times of roughly seconds for o3-mini versus tens of seconds for o1. He then uses o3-mini-high to generate a Chrome extension in about 9 seconds of thinking, copies the files into an editor and loads them into the browser's extensions tab, and notes one drawback: the extension sometimes distorts images on the page. He closes by saying the model is also available in Cursor and Windsurf, which he says Windsurf announced but which he has not seen himself. The evidence is a single run per prompt with no repeats, no accuracy counts and no prompt text shared, so it supports only the anecdote that o3-mini is fast on simple puzzles.

key_ideas.idea: o3-mini and o3-mini-high are rolled out to ChatGPT Plus, Team and Pro users via the model dropdown; free users can try reasoning through the 'Reason' option, with less control over which model runs.
key_ideas.detail: Access tiers as stated in the video, not checked against OpenAI's documentation.

key_ideas.idea: The speaker cites OpenAI's benchmarks claiming o3-mini-high beats o1 on math, PhD-level science and coding, then sets them aside to run his own test.
key_ideas.detail: The benchmark claim is a vendor claim that the host repeats without numbers.

key_ideas.idea: On six short reasoning prompts, o3-mini (standard tier) gave answers the speaker judged correct, with much shorter response times than o1 as he recalls them.
key_ideas.detail: Reported times: jug puzzle 7s versus roughly 40-50s for o1; river crossing 13s; candle order 23s versus about a minute; word frequency 10s. These are single runs, timed by eye, and o1 times come from memory.

key_ideas.idea: The speaker picked the standard o3-mini over o3-mini-high for the puzzles, reasoning that the lower tier should respond faster, and found it still got these prompts right.
key_ideas.detail: Tier choice is a latency tradeoff. On these simple puzzles the lower tier was enough, according to the speaker. He does not test harder problems where the higher tier might differ.

key_ideas.idea: Counting kiwis took under a second with o3-mini versus about 50 seconds with o1, which counted items one by one. The probability question was also answered in a couple of seconds.
key_ideas.detail: This is the most vivid latency contrast in the video, but it comes from one prompt.

key_ideas.idea: The model generated a working Chrome extension from o3-mini-high in about 9 seconds of thinking. The speaker copied the files into an editor and loaded them into the browser's extensions tab.
key_ideas.detail: The result had one visible defect: on some pages the extension distorted images. The speaker does not show the prompt used.

key_ideas.idea: The speaker says the model is available in Cursor, and that Windsurf announced support, which he has not seen in its product yet.
key_ideas.detail: Integration claims are second-hand. He did not verify them.

techniques.name: Latency-first spot check of a reasoning model
techniques.how: Write a small set of short reasoning prompts with known answers (liquid-measuring puzzle, river crossing with constraints, candle burn order, counting items, word-frequency count, a simple probability problem). Run each on the new model and on the previous reasoning model, and time the response from prompt to answer. Record correctness and seconds for each.
techniques.when: When you want a quick feel for whether a new reasoning model is faster on simple tasks before a fuller eval. Use it as a screen only, since the video's own run is one attempt per prompt with no repeats.

techniques.name: Pick the lower reasoning tier when the task is simple
techniques.how: In the ChatGPT model picker, choose the standard o3-mini instead of o3-mini-high for routine puzzles. The speaker's rule of thumb is that the lower tier responds faster and can still be correct on easy problems.
techniques.when: For latency-sensitive steps that involve simple logic or counting. Escalate to the high tier only when the lower tier gives wrong answers on your own prompts.

techniques.name: One-shot scaffold for a small browser extension
techniques.how: Ask the high-reasoning model to create a Chrome extension in one prompt. Copy each generated file into a project folder, then load the extension from the browser's extensions tab. Test on real pages, since the speaker found the extension changed how images displayed on some sites.
techniques.when: For quick prototypes of small browser tools, where a generated skeleton saves time and the rough edges are acceptable. Not a substitute for review or testing on target sites.

numbers.claim: o3-mini answered a jug-measuring puzzle (1L and 2L jugs, measure 3L) in about 7 seconds; the speaker recalls o1 taking roughly 40-50 seconds.
o3-mini solved a river-crossing puzzle (boat carries one person and two animals) in 13 seconds with one crossing given as the minimum.
o3-mini took 23 seconds on a candle puzzle; the speaker recalls o1 taking about a minute.
Counting kiwis took under 1 second with o3-mini versus about 50 seconds with o1, which counted each item.
A word-frequency prompt took 10 seconds with o3-mini standard.
o3-mini-high spent about 9 seconds thinking before generating a complete Chrome extension.
Six reasoning prompts were tested in total, each one run once. The video does not report accuracy as a fraction, but the speaker says all were correct.

hot_takes: Title asks 'the fastest reasoning model yet?' but the test is six prompts run once each, timed by eye, against o1 times recalled from memory.
The 'fastest' claim is about easy puzzles on the lower tier; the speaker does not test harder reasoning where speed could cost accuracy.
Speaker calls the model a 'game changer for more complex tasks' but his only complex-ish task was a one-shot Chrome extension with a visible image bug.
Benchmark claims from OpenAI are repeated as framing and then set aside without checking.

relevance.action: If strategy routing gains a reasoning-tier option, add per-model time-to-answer as a routing signal and measure it on your own prompts instead of trusting vendor benchmarks.

relevance.why: ProsHarness uses a second model for critique. A fast reasoning tier could be a cheaper critic option, but this talk offers no evidence on critique quality.
relevance.action: Consider o3-mini as an alternative critic in a plan-critique loop only if you can run your own critique-quality eval first.
